hardware: Windows laptop Intel i7-1165G7 @ 2.80GHz with Chrome 116; Apple M2 MacBook Air with Firefox 117
name: DuckDB-Wasm
language: C++ (DuckDB compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten) with a TypeScript API
baseline: Arquero and Danfo.js (pure-JS in-browser dataframe libraries) and SQLite WASM; the VLDB paper names sql.js, Arquero and Lovefield as the previous Web data-processing libraries
workload: In-browser analytical queries (top-level metrics, group by day, top 5 countries by item, 10 random rows) over a sales dataset, run in Chrome 116 and Firefox 117; the VLDB paper runs TPC-H at several scale factors against other Web libraries.
claimed_speedup: VLDB 2022 paper abstract (seen only in search snippets): outperforms previous data processing libraries for the Web on TPC-H at multiple scale factors. Independent repo, Chrome 116, i7-1165G7, timings (unit not stated): group by day 1.05 Arquero vs 0.163 DuckDB WASM (6.4x, derived from page data); top 5 countries 4.847 vs 0.114 (42x, derived from page data); top-level metrics 0.067 vs 0.014 (4.8x, derived from page data); 10 random rows 0.517 vs 0.032 (16x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: WASM build has a large download compared with pure-JS libraries. In the same independent repo it loses on load and write paths: load data 4.309 vs SQLite WASM 0.893 (Chrome), insert 1000 rows 1.397 vs 0.041, update 1000 rows 0.588 vs 0.038, delete 1000 rows 2.376 vs 0.035. It is an analytical (OLAP) engine, so point writes are not its strength.
caveats: The VLDB PDF (vldb.org) and duckdb.org were not reachable (egress blocked); the paper claim comes from a search snippet and the tier B rests on peer review plus the independent repo numbers. The timing unit in the independent repo is not stated, it is a single run on one machine per browser (7 stars), and the README itself says fetch/load timings are noisy. No comparison against native DuckDB was found. The repo has benchmark source in packages/benchmarks (TPC-H scripts) that was listed but not opened; CPU, compiler flags and scale-factor results of the paper are unconfirmed.
found_via: WebSearch: 'DuckDB-Wasm paper in-browser analytical SQL performance evaluation vs native DuckDB and JavaScript libraries'; follow-up search for TPC-H libraries

hardware: Per-device table: iPhone X/XS, Pixel 4, ThinkPad X1 Gen6 (Linux), Windows desktop, MacBook Pro 15 2019; CPU models not given; Chrome 79.0
name: TensorFlow.js WASM backend (tfjs-backend-wasm)
language: C++ (XNNPACK) compiled to WebAssembly with a TypeScript API
baseline: TensorFlow.js plain JS (CPU) backend in the browser; the WebGL backend is also reported
workload: MobileNet V2 (~300M multiply-adds) and Face Detector (~20M multiply-adds) inference, averaged across 200 runs, Chrome 79.0 on several phones and desktops.
claimed_speedup: README: for MobileNet V2 the WASM backend is 'between ~3X-11.5X faster than the plain JS backend' and '~5.3-7.7X slower than the WebGL backend'; for Face Detector '~8.2-19.8X faster than the plain JS backend'. With SIMD and threads, MacBook Pro 15 2019 MobileNet V2: 10.3 ms vs 893.5 ms plain JS (86.7x, derived from page data); ThinkPad X1 Gen6 12.4 ms vs 1489.4 ms (120x, derived from page data); Face Detector desktop Linux 6.2 ms vs 249.5 ms.
tradeoffs: SIMD and multi-threaded builds need browser support (README: without them the backend falls back to plain WASM or SIMD only) and threads need cross-origin isolation. For medium models (100-500M multiply-adds) the WASM backend is several times slower than WebGL; for lite models (20-60M) it is comparable. Better numerical stability and wider device support than WebGL.
caveats: First-party Google numbers from Chrome 79 (2020), now old. The 'plain JS' baseline is TensorFlow.js's own unoptimized CPU backend, not a native TensorFlow baseline. The Node v14 row was not measured in Chrome. The benchmark page (tfjs-benchmarks.web.app) and the SIMD/threads blog post (blog.tensorflow.org) were not opened (egress blocked). Compiler flags not on the page. The repo-wide last commit date is shown, not the backend's.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly SIMD library speedup over JavaScript implementation benchmark github README' (TensorFlow blog snippet); README opened at github.com

name: hash-wasm
language: WebAssembly binaries with a TypeScript API
baseline: Pure-JS hash libraries: spark-md5 3.0.2 (MD5), jsSHA 3.3.1 (SHA1), noble-hashes 1.3.2 (SHA256, PBKDF2), xxhashjs 0.2.2 (XXHash64); wasm libraries sha256-wasm, xxhash-wasm and argon2-browser
workload: Hashing 32-byte and 1 MB inputs in Chrome v131 (MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA3-512, XXHash64), PBKDF2-SHA512 with 1000 iterations, Argon2id m=512 t=8 p=1.
claimed_speedup: MD5 1 MB 850.31 MB/s vs spark-md5 171.73 MB/s (4.95x, derived from page data); SHA1 1 MB 798.19 vs jsSHA 78.12 MB/s (10.2x, derived); SHA256 1 MB 426.16 vs noble-hashes 110.02 MB/s (3.9x, derived) and vs sha256-wasm 308.39 MB/s (1.4x, derived); XXHash64 1 MB 15,989 MB/s vs xxhashjs 42.26 MB/s (378x, derived) but equal to xxhash-wasm 15,929 MB/s; Argon2id 438 ops vs argon2-browser 213 ops (2.1x, derived); PBKDF2-SHA512 588 ops vs noble-hashes 395 ops (1.5x, derived).
tradeoffs: Browser and Node.js library with an async init step for the wasm module. It was not compared with Node's native crypto module (which would be far faster in Node) or with WebCrypto.
caveats: First-party README numbers (Chrome only, one machine). Competitor versions are pinned to older releases (for example noble-hashes 1.3.2, xxhash-wasm 1.0.2). The benchmark app lives in a separate repo (Daninet/hash-wasm-benchmark) that shows no licence and whose JS source was not confirmed; the wasm compiler flags were not on the README page, so the tier stays C. Only 1.0x gain over xxhash-wasm on 1 MB XXHash64.
found_via: Direct github.com README fetch after WebSearch rounds on wasm-vs-JS libraries ('WebAssembly SIMD library speedup over JavaScript implementation benchmark github README')

hardware: Not stated for the xxhashjs comparison; 'x64 MacBook Pro running Node 17.3' is named only for the Node crypto comparison
name: xxhash-wasm
baseline: xxhashjs (pure-JS xxHash); README also compares Node's crypto module
workload: Hashing random strings of 1 byte up to 100,000,000 bytes with Benchmark.js, 32-bit and 64-bit variants.
claimed_speedup: README: 'the 32-bit is up to 90 times faster' and 'the 64-bit is up to 350 times faster' than xxhashjs. 1 byte: xxhashjs 32-bit 513,517 ops/s vs xxhash-wasm 5,752,446 ops/s (11x, derived from page data); 100,000,000 bytes: xxhashjs 32-bit 0.31 vs 27.84 ops/s (90x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Port of the xxHash algorithm (cyan4973/xxhash is already catalogued), so it may fold into that entry as a wrapper. Needs async wasm initialization.
caveats: First-party; compiler flags and CPU model missing for the headline xxhashjs numbers; xxhashjs is an old, slow pure-JS baseline, so the ratio overstates the gain over a tuned JS xxHash. hash-wasm's XXHash64 matches it on 1 MB (15,989 vs 15,929 MB/s per hash-wasm README).
found_via: Direct github.com README fetch after WebSearch rounds on wasm-vs-JS libraries; surfaced next to hash-wasm benchmark tables

hardware: 2.9 GHz MacBook, macOS 10.15, Node.js v14.11.0 (CPU model not given)
name: markdown-wasm
language: C (md4c) compiled to WebAssembly with a JavaScript API
baseline: markdown-it, marked, commonmark.js and showdown (pure-JS Markdown parsers) in Node.js
workload: Parse and render to HTML a set of sample markdown files (benchmark suite adapted from commonmark.js bench), single thread, Node.js.
claimed_speedup: Average ops/second: markdown-wasm 195,065; markdown-it 84,774; marked 76,942; commonmark 66,185; showdown 8,502 (2.3x over markdown-it, derived from page data). Average throughput: markdown-wasm 49 MB/s vs markdown-it 17, commonmark 16, marked 14, showdown 2 MB/s (2.9x over markdown-it, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: 31 kB gzipped, CommonMark via md4c; no plugin ecosystem comparable to markdown-it; output follows md4c, not identical to the JS parsers.
caveats: First-party results sit in SVG charts, the numbers above were read from the SVG text (label and value order assumed aligned). Measured on Node, not in a browser, with 2020 versions of the JS parsers (markdown-it ^10, marked ^0.7, commonmark ^0.29.2, showdown ^1.9.1 per the benchmark package.json). Wasm build flags and CPU model unstated. Repo has had no commits since 2021.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/rsms/markdown-wasm after WebSearch rounds on wasm-vs-JS libraries; benchmark SVGs fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Loro
language: Rust compiled to WebAssembly with JavaScript bindings
baseline: Yjs 13.6.11 (pure-JS CRDT library); the same table also lists ywasm 0.9.3 and Automerge 2.1.10 (both wasm)
workload: dmonad/crdt-benchmarks suite on Node 20.5.0: B1 no conflicts, B2 two users with conflicts, B3 many conflicts, B4 replay of a real-world editing trace (259,778 operations) at N=6000.
claimed_speedup: B4 apply real-world editing dataset: loro 0.10.1 3,089 ms vs yjs 5,714 ms (1.85x, derived from page data); B4 parseTime 13 ms vs 39 ms; B1.1 append N characters 120 ms vs 188 ms; B3.1 56 ms vs 75 ms. Mixed: Yjs is faster on B2.2 (65 ms vs 83 ms), B2.4 (178 vs 208 ms) and B3.4 (72 vs 227 ms).
tradeoffs: Bundle size 1,052,250 bytes vs Yjs 69,124 bytes; larger update messages (B1.1 average update size 109 vs 27 bytes). Compared with ywasm and Automerge (both wasm) Loro is also faster on B4 (28,675 ms and 14,326 ms).
caveats: Third-party shootout maintained by the Yjs author, so the competitor ran it; wasm compiler flags are not stated in the table. Measured Loro version 0.10.1 is older than the current release. Loro's snapshot feature is enabled by default in the harness and affects parseTime; memUsed does not include wasm runtime memory. Gains are workload-specific (Yjs wins several conflict workloads).
found_via: Direct github.com fetch of dmonad/crdt-benchmarks README while searching wasm libraries vs JS equivalents

name: absurd-sql
language: JavaScript backend for SQLite compiled to WebAssembly (sql.js)
baseline: IndexedDB used directly in the browser
workload: SQLite on top of IndexedDB blocks: read 'SELECT SUM(value) FROM kv' and bulk insert, compared with plain IndexedDB, in Chrome.
claimed_speedup: README: 'It consistently beats IndexedDB performance up to 10x' for reads and bulk-insert writes (shown only as chart images, no numbers readable).
tradeoffs: Needs SharedArrayBuffer (cross-origin isolation headers); Safari fallback allows only one writing tab at a time; relies on sql.js (SQLite WASM).
caveats: First-party charts only, numbers not in text; baseline is the IndexedDB browser API rather than a JS library, so this is a storage-layer win, not a wasm compute win. Benchmark code is in src/examples/bench but was not opened. Repo unmaintained since 2023.
found_via: Direct github.com README fetch while searching wasm libraries vs in-browser incumbents (WebSearch 'WebAssembly port of library faster than native...')

hardware: Intel Kaby Lake desktop CPU (exact model not given), Node.js v16.14
name: gmp-wasm
language: C (GMP and MPFR) compiled to WebAssembly with a TypeScript API
baseline: JavaScript built-in BigInt (also big-integer 1.6.51 and decimal.js 10.3.1)
workload: Computing digits of pi with a series (benchmark/calcpi.js) using arbitrary-precision Integer and Float types, Node.js v16.14.
claimed_speedup: Integer() high-level wrapper 88 ms vs BigInt 129 ms (1.47x); with delayed deallocation 78 ms (1.65x); MPZ low-level functions 53 ms (2.43x); Float() high-level wrapper 175 ms (0.74x, slower than baseline); MPFR low-level 118 ms (1.09x); Float(1).atan().mul(4) listed at 215x and Float('0.5').asin().mul(6) at 7.59x.
tradeoffs: Manual memory management and deallocation concerns (README suggests reinitializing the bindings); LGPL-3.0; bundled wasm binary; offers Rational and Float types and many more operations than BigInt.
caveats: First-party; baseline for the 215x and 7.59x rows is not stated on the page; the high-level Float wrapper is slower than the baseline. CPU model and compiler flags missing. Benchmark source (benchmark/calcpi.js) is linked but was not opened. Node 16 is old.
found_via: Direct github.com README fetch after WebSearch rounds on wasm-vs-JS libraries (same author as hash-wasm)

name: Harper
workload: Linting a moderate-size English document; memory footprint compared with LanguageTool.
claimed_speedup: README (author claim, no benchmark): takes milliseconds to lint a document while LanguageTool 'would take several seconds'; uses 'less than 1/50th of LanguageTool's memory footprint'.
tradeoffs: English only; far fewer rules than LanguageTool and no n-gram data set; the WebAssembly build is one delivery target alongside native binaries and a language server.
caveats: Claim is not wasm-versus-native: the baseline is a native Java tool and the speedup is not tied to the wasm build. No benchmark code, hardware or document size given; 'milliseconds' is not quantified. Low fit for this category.
found_via: github.com/topics/webassembly sorted by stars, then README fetch
